label: Horizon
blurb: Build, script, and publish VR worlds in Meta Horizon Worlds using the desktop editor, Horizon Studio.

lessons.title: What Is Horizon Worlds?
lessons.subtitle: Two ways to build: VR or desktop
steps: Horizon Worlds is Meta's platform for building and playing social VR spaces.
You can visit on a Quest headset, or on a phone and PC screen.
There are two ways to build: in VR, or on a PC with the desktop editor.
The in-VR creation tools were retired. Serious building now happens on PC.
The PC app, called Horizon Studio, is where this guide works.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: You still test in VR, but you build, script, and publish from the desktop editor.

quiz.q: Where does serious building happen now?

lessons.title: Get Horizon Studio
lessons.subtitle: Download and open the desktop editor
steps: Horizon Studio is a free flatscreen app for Windows PCs.
Download it from the Meta Horizon website or the Meta Quest app.
Install it, then log in with the same Meta account you play with.
Open the app to see your worlds and the Create button.
You do not need a headset on to build, only to test in true VR.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Horizon Studio is the 2025 name for what builders used to call the Desktop Editor.

quiz.q: Horizon Studio runs on which device?

lessons.title: The Horizon Studio Layout
lessons.subtitle: Viewport, Hierarchy, Properties, more
steps: The Viewport in the middle is your 3D world. You look and build here.
The Hierarchy lists every object in the scene, like a table of contents.
The Properties panel shows settings for whatever object you select.
The Asset Library holds shapes, models, sounds, and your uploads.
The Console prints messages and errors while you test.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Panels can be moved and resized. If one goes missing, reopen it from the top menu.

quiz.q: Which panel lists every object in your scene?

lessons.title: Moving Around the Editor
lessons.subtitle: Desktop keys vs grabbing in VR
steps: On desktop, press W A S D to fly forward, back, and sideways.
Hold the right mouse button and drag to look around.
Click an object, then press F to focus the camera on it.
Scroll the mouse wheel to zoom the view in and out.
In VR you move differently: reach out, grab an object, and pull it.
To scale in VR, grab with both hands and move them apart or together.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Desktop is precise and fast for layout. VR is great for checking real scale and feel.

quiz.q: How do you look around on the desktop?

lessons.title: Create a New World
lessons.subtitle: Start from an empty scene
steps: From the Studio home screen, click Create to start a new world.
Pick a template or choose an empty world to start from scratch.
An empty scene is just a floor, the sky, and a spawn point.
Give the world a clear name so you can find it again.
Open the world to load the scene into the editor.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Starting empty teaches you the most. Templates are handy once you know the basics.

quiz.q: What is in a fresh empty world?
choices: A floor, sky, and spawn point

lessons.title: Add Objects and Shapes
lessons.subtitle: Drop in cubes, spheres, and more
steps: Open the Asset Library to find build blocks and ready-made models.
Start with primitives: cube, sphere, cylinder, and flat shapes.
Drag an asset into the Viewport, or select it and click to place it.
Each object you add shows up as a new line in the Hierarchy.
Combine simple primitives to rough out walls, floors, and props.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Gray-box your world with plain cubes first. Add nice models once layout feels right.

quiz.q: What is a primitive?

lessons.title: Move, Rotate, Scale
lessons.subtitle: The gizmo handles and grid snap
steps: Select an object to see its gizmo: a set of colored handles.
Drag the arrows to move it along one direction.
Drag the curved rings to rotate it.
Drag the small boxes to scale it bigger or smaller.
Turn on grid snapping so objects line up to even steps.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Snapping keeps walls flush and floors aligned. Toggle it off for loose placement.

quiz.q: What do the ring handles do?

lessons.title: The Hierarchy Window
lessons.subtitle: Parent, group, name, and lock
steps: The Hierarchy is the list of every object, nested like folders.
Drag one object onto another to parent it. Children follow the parent.
Group related objects into a folder to keep the list tidy.
Double-click a name to rename it. Clear names save you time later.
Lock an object so you do not move it by accident while building.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Parent a lamp to a table, and moving the table carries the lamp along with it.

quiz.q: What happens when you parent object A to B?
choices: A follows B when B moves

lessons.title: The Properties Panel
lessons.subtitle: Transform, color, and collision
steps: Select an object and the Properties panel fills with its settings.
Transform sets position, rotation, and scale as exact numbers.
Material and color change how the surface looks.
Visibility can hide an object from players while you keep it in the scene.
Collision decides if players and objects can pass through it or not.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Type exact transform numbers for precise placement that dragging cannot match.

quiz.q: What does turning off collision do?

lessons.title: The Asset Library
lessons.subtitle: Built-in assets and your uploads
steps: The Asset Library is your shelf of shapes, models, sounds, and effects.
Built-in assets come free with Horizon and are ready to drag in.
Your Uploads holds custom models and textures you brought in.
Use the search box to find an asset by name fast.
Every asset has a numeric Asset ID. Scripts use that ID to spawn it.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Note an asset's ID when you plan to spawn it from a script later, like a sound.

quiz.q: What is an Asset ID?
choices: A number that names an asset

lessons.title: Import a 3D Model
lessons.subtitle: Upload FBX and PNG together
steps: Model in Blender or another tool, then export the mesh as an FBX file.
Save your textures as PNG images next to the FBX.
In Horizon Studio, open Your Uploads and start a new import.
Upload the FBX and its PNG textures together so they link up.
Once processed, drag your model from the Asset Library into the world.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Keep the model light: fewer polygons and smaller textures load faster for players.

quiz.q: Which files do you upload together for a model?

lessons.title: Gizmos You Use a Lot
lessons.subtitle: Text, triggers, spawns, and more
steps: A gizmo is a special object that adds behavior, not just a shape.
Text shows words in the world. Trigger Zone fires when a player enters.
Spawn Point sets where players appear when they arrive.
Door lets players move between areas. Particle adds effects like smoke.
Audio plays sound. Drag a gizmo in from the Asset Library like any asset.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Triggers are the start of most interactivity: enter a zone, and something happens.

quiz.q: What does a Trigger Zone do?

lessons.title: Add Sound and Ambience
lessons.subtitle: Spawn audio to fill your world
steps: Sound in Horizon plays through an Audio gizmo, driven by an audio asset.
Find or upload an audio asset and note its numeric Asset ID.
The common way is to spawn that asset as an AudioGizmo from a script.
Set it to loop for steady background ambience like wind or music.
Place point sounds near objects so they fade with distance.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Layer a soft looping ambience under short one-shot sounds for a world that feels alive.

quiz.q: How do you usually play a sound asset?

lessons.title: The Scripts Panel
lessons.subtitle: Attach TypeScript and set modes
steps: Scripts add logic in TypeScript. You cannot edit scripts in VR, only on desktop.
Horizon uses strict TypeScript, CommonJS, ES2020, around version 4.7.
Create a script in the Scripts panel, then attach it to an object.
Server and game logic use Execution Mode Default on an empty object.
Local mode runs on one player's own device. Noesis UI panels run Shared.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Put core game rules in one Default script on an empty object, kept away from art.

quiz.q: Which mode runs server and game logic?

lessons.title: Saves and Leaderboards
lessons.subtitle: Keep scores with persistent data
steps: To remember a player's progress, use Horizon persistent variables.
A persistent variable stores data per player that survives between visits.
Use a leaderboard to track and rank scores across players.
Read and write these from your scripts when a player earns points.
Do not build your own ranking board in a panel. Use the real leaderboard.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Persistent variables are for saves. Leaderboards are for scores. Never fake them in UI.

quiz.q: Where should scores be ranked?

lessons.title: Custom UI With Noesis
lessons.subtitle: Panels for menus and buttons
steps: Noesis panels are custom screens: menus, buttons, scoreboards, and more.
First open Scripts, then Script Settings, then API, and enable horizon/ui.
Also enable horizon/noesis, or your panels will not connect at all.
Build the panel layout, then drive it with a script that runs Shared.
Buttons send events to your logic, and the panel updates what players see.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: The enable-the-API step is the one everyone forgets. No API, no panel. Do it first.

quiz.q: What must you enable before a Noesis panel works?

lessons.title: Test With Play Mode
lessons.subtitle: Preview your world and read logs
steps: Press Play or Preview to drop into your world and try it as a player.
Walk around, press buttons, and check that triggers and sounds fire.
Watch the Console for errors and for messages your scripts print.
Stop play to return to editing with your changes still in place.
Test in a headset too, since VR scale and comfort can feel different.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Read the Console first when something breaks. The error names the script and line.

quiz.q: Where do script errors show up?

lessons.title: Keep Your World Light
lessons.subtitle: Performance and the sim budget
steps: Every object, script, and effect costs performance. Lighter worlds run smoother.
Use fewer objects and simpler meshes. Merge small props where you can.
Keep textures modest in size so they load fast on a headset.
Watch the simulation budget. Going over it causes lag and dropped frames.
Turn off collision and physics on objects that do not need them.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Build for the headset, not your PC. A Quest has far less power than a gaming rig.

quiz.q: Why keep a world light?

lessons.title: Share and Protect a World
lessons.subtitle: Editors, testers, and your work
steps: Invite collaborators from the world's sharing settings.
An Editor can build, edit, and copy the whole world.
A Tester can only enter and play to give you feedback.
Only add trusted people as Editors, since they can copy everything.
A copy can be re-shared, so guard original art, scripts, and ideas.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Give feedback-only helpers the Tester role. Save the Editor role for build partners.

quiz.q: Who can copy your whole world?

lessons.title: Publish Your World
lessons.subtitle: Preview images and going live
steps: Publishing makes your world public so anyone can find and play it.
Prepare three preview images at 2560x1440, 1440x1440, and 810x1440.
Each preview image must be under 4MB. Trim the file size if it is bigger.
Fill in world settings: name, description, and player limits.
Review everything, then publish. Update any time by publishing again.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Strong preview images sell your world in the feed. Treat them like a movie poster.

quiz.q: Which preview image size is required?
